{"id": "26:218/q10", "question": "What does reliance on God require or consist of?", "turns_on": "The descriptions emphasize knowledge, faith, dependence, certainty, exclusive hope, or servanthood; two reports differ on whether reliance's reality can be captured through description.", "positions": [{"id": "26:218/q10/p1", "position": "Outwardly it follows knowledge; inwardly it puts certainty into practice.", "reasons": "Al-Kattānī distinguishes outward, inward, and true realization of reliance."}, {"id": "26:218/q10/p2", "position": "It accompanies faith and grows with it through discipline, patience, and God's aid.", "reasons": "Abū al-Ḥusayn al-Rāzī says seeking reliance entails preserving faith, disciplining the self by its rules, practicing patience, and seeking divine help."}, {"id": "26:218/q10/p3", "position": "It is the heart's dependence on God within the covenant of faith.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿUyayna identifies this inward dependence as part of faith's covenant."}, {"id": "26:218/q10/p4", "position": "Its reality cannot be known through description alone.", "reasons": "An unnamed authority calls reliance part of the covenant of faith but denies that description alone discloses its reality; Abū Sulaymān al-Dārānī contrasts his own access through its defining quality."}, {"id": "26:218/q10/p5", "position": "It can be known through its defining quality.", "reasons": "Abū Sulaymān al-Dārānī says this in express contrast to the claim that its reality eludes description."}, {"id": "26:218/q10/p6", "position": "It is strength grounded in dependence and certainty.", "reasons": "Reported from an unnamed authority by al-Sulamī."}, {"id": "26:218/q10/p7", "position": "It abandons fear and hope in anyone besides God.", "reasons": "Reported from an unnamed authority by al-Sulamī."}, {"id": "26:218/q10/p8", "position": "It subjects the self to servanthood and fixes the heart and gaze on God.", "reasons": "An unnamed authority places the heart with lordship and directs one's whole gaze to God."}]}
{"id": "26:218/q11", "question": "Does the adjoining description of movement among prostrators support believing ancestors?", "turns_on": "Whether 'movement among prostrators' may refer to ancestral transmission, whether 'father' in 6:74 can be shifted to uncle or maternal grandfather, and whether the pure-loins report can outweigh the Qurʾānic wording.", "positions": [{"id": "26:218/q11/p1", "position": "Yes: it can describe the Prophet's soul passing through a line of believing ancestors.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī reports the Rāfiḍa's inference from movement among prostrators. They cite the ungraded report of transfer through pure loins and wombs and 9:28's description of unbelievers as impure. To meet 6:74's naming of Āzar as Abraham's father, they say 'father' can mean uncle, citing Ishmael as father of Jacob's sons in 2:133 and the Prophet's calling al-ʿAbbās father; or maternal grandfather, citing Jesus among Abraham's descendants in 6:84–85. Al-Rāzī objects that this departs from the apparent sense, combines possible senses of an ambiguous term, and sets a solitary report against the Qurʾān."}, {"id": "26:218/q11/p2", "position": "No: the ancestry inference fails against the apparent wording and cannot be established by that report.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī retains the apparent 'his father Āzar' in 6:74; he rejects making one ambiguous expression carry all possible senses at once and says the solitary pure-loins report cannot outweigh the Qurʾān."}]}
{"id": "26:218/q12", "question": "What other readings of 'when you rise' are reported without detail?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "26:218/q12/p1", "position": "Exegetes offer various other possibilities, but this note does not specify them.", "reasons": "Iṣlāḥī acknowledges unspecified exegetical alternatives before preferring the tahajjud reading."}]}
{"id": "26:219/q01", "question": "What does taqallub mean as a word?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "26:219/q01/p1", "position": "Turning or moving about, including coming and going.", "reasons": "Jishumī derives it from turning something over by hand or turning oneself; Bursevī applies the movement to rounds of inspection, and Iṣlāḥī calls it coming and going."}]}
{"id": "26:219/q02", "question": "How does the accusative taqallubaka connect to the preceding verb?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "26:219/q02/p1", "position": "It is a verbal noun object coordinated with the object of 'He sees': He sees you and your turning.", "reasons": "Jishumī supplies an understood yarā, while al-Samīn and Abū Ḥayyān describe coordination with the object of yarāka; Abū Ḥayyān identifies this as the majority reading's syntax."}]}
{"id": "26:219/q03", "question": "What variant verbal reading is reported here?", "turns_on": "The transmitted verbal form and person, in contrast with the common nominal reading.", "positions": [{"id": "26:219/q03/p1", "position": "Junāḥ ibn Ḥubaysh reads wa-yuqallibuka, 'and He turns you.'", "reasons": "Al-Samīn specifies the doubled lām and coordination with yarāka; Abū Ḥayyān reports it as a present verb coordinated with yarāka. Ālūsī says it may coordinate with yarāka or taqūm and takes the turning to suggest complete, concentrated prayer."}, {"id": "26:219/q03/p2", "position": "A first-person plural reading has wa-nuqallibuka, 'and We turn you.'", "reasons": "Rāzī reports this form."}]}
{"id": "26:219/q04", "question": "What does the Prophet's turning among the prostrators describe?", "turns_on": "Whether turning denotes prayer postures, rounds of worshippers, rearward sight, activity among believers, ancestral or prophetic passage, or an inward movement; several authors weigh the apparent wording and surrounding time frame.", "positions": [{"id": "26:219/q04/p1", "position": "His prayer movements among worshippers, especially while leading the congregation.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿIkrima, al-Farrāʾ and others enumerate standing, bowing, prostration and sometimes sitting; Qatāda, Muqātil and others distinguish God seeing him alone and with the congregation. Al-Ṭabarī prefers this as the apparent wording; Ibn ʿAṭiyya calls prayer apparent, and al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī prefers congregational prayer. Ālūsī connects full movement with concentrated humility."}, {"id": "26:219/q04/p2", "position": "His visits to inspect companions engaged in night worship.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī, al-Nasafī and others relate this to the Prophet's own night prayer, the worshippers' work for the afterlife, and his unobtrusive inspection. Iṣlāḥī places visits in the mosque and relates them to his care for followers."}, {"id": "26:219/q04/p3", "position": "His gaze moving over worshippers behind him, whom he could see during prayer.", "reasons": "Mujāhid's explanation is supported by reports of the Prophet seeing those behind as clearly as those ahead; Study Quran compares turning the face in 2:144. Ibn ʿAṭiyya rejects the connection to this passage; al-Qurṭubī accepts the vision report but calls this interpretation remote; Ālūsī also deems it far-fetched."}, {"id": "26:219/q04/p4", "position": "His movements and changing states among believing companions generally.", "reasons": "Al-Ḥasan explains movements and travels among believers; Ibn ʿAbbās and Qatāda can describe believers as prostrators. Asad contrasts the believers with disobedient people in 26:216. Al-Ṭabarī rejects movement merely among people as distant from the ordinary sense of prostration, though all things and their shadows prostrate."}, {"id": "26:219/q04/p5", "position": "His activity among believers while managing religion and advancing God's word.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī relates it to affairs and rulings among Muslims, paired with rising to fight polytheists; al-Zamakhsharī, Rāzī and Abū Ḥayyān stress that no state is hidden from God. Ālūsī describes proclamation, and Elmalılı service among believers."}, {"id": "26:219/q04/p6", "position": "His passage through the loins of prophetic or monotheist forebears until his birth.", "reasons": "Reports name Adam, Noah and Abraham and sometimes say lawful marriage without fornication; some speak of his light or spirit. Bursevī allows intervening nonprophetic ancestors. Elmalılı objects that ancestral transfer is past while the context concerns present and future; Ālūsī says this lineage interpretation cannot establish the parents' faith."}, {"id": "26:219/q04/p7", "position": "His conduct in the states and mission of earlier prophets.", "reasons": "Saʿīd ibn Jubayr compares the Prophet's activity to earlier prophets; Elmalılı calls it service in the prophetic office. Ālūsī dismisses this reading as far-fetched."}, {"id": "26:219/q04/p8", "position": "His remembrance and description passing over the tongues of earlier prophets.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī transmits this further interpretation."}, {"id": "26:219/q04/p9", "position": "His being alone in private devotion.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzī reports this from al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī."}, {"id": "26:219/q04/p10", "position": "An inward turning of the Prophet's attributes through saints and prophets.", "reasons": "Al-Sulamī transmits an unnamed inward reading."}, {"id": "26:219/q04/p11", "position": "The inward secret's continual turning in divine nearness.", "reasons": "Al-Sulamī's unnamed source associates prostration with intimacy and nearness, citing 96:19; al-Sulamī describes continual turning in the sanctified place of witnessed presence."}, {"id": "26:219/q04/p12", "position": "His progress through annihilation in God's acts, attributes and essence, through self, heart and spirit.", "reasons": "Al-Qāshānī locates this turning among those already annihilated in God."}, {"id": "26:219/q04/p13", "position": "His place among prostrating spirits created from his spirit.", "reasons": "Bursevī transmits a mystical saying that God knew his mastery of Adam's children and worthiness of honor."}]}

Al-Ṭabarī says ordinary usage points to familiar prostration; Ālūsī explains their designation by prostration's special nearness to God and its rank as the best pillar according to many imams."}, {"id": "26:219/q05/p2", "position": "Believers generally, among whom the Prophet moves.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās and Qatāda call believers prostrators; Asad contrasts believers with those disobeying him at 26:216. Al-Ṭabarī argues broad reference to people departs from the phrase's ordinary sense."}, {"id": "26:219/q05/p3", "position": "The earlier prophets or monotheist forebears.", "reasons": "Saʿīd ibn Jubayr understands prophetic conduct; lineage reports refer to prophetic or believing loins. Ālūsī dismisses the prophetic-conduct reading as far-fetched; Elmalılı rejects the ancestral reading because its past time jars with the context."}, {"id": "26:219/q05/p4", "position": "Worshippers' spirits in the world of spirits.", "reasons": "Bursevī transmits that each spirit was created from the Prophet's spirit."}]}
{"id": "26:219/q06", "question": "What did the Prophet say or do concerning worshippers behind him?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "26:219/q06/p1", "position": "He said he saw worshippers behind his back as clearly as those before him and instructed them to straighten their rows or complete their bowing and prostration.", "reasons": "Anas, Abū Hurayra, Jābir from al-Bāqir and other reports vary in the instruction: align or close rows, complete bowing and prostration, or do not precede him in rising and bowing. Al-Qurṭubī calls the vision report authentic, Ibn Kathīr sound, Ālūsī locates Anas in al-Bukhārī and Abū Hurayra in Abū Dāwūd; Rāzī and Study Quran give no grading. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī explains the rising as lifting the forehead from prostration."}]}
{"id": "26:219/q07", "question": "What is reported about his visits after the night vigil duty ended?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "26:219/q07/p1", "position": "He visited companions' homes to inspect their continuing worship and heard recitation and remembrance buzzing like wasps or bees.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī, Rāzī, al-Bayḍāwī, Abū Ḥayyān, Bursevī, Ālūsī and Study Quran relate the same account; Rāzī gives no grading. Bursevī says the five prayers on the Night Journey lifted the obligation."}]}
{"id": "26:219/q08", "question": "What obligation of night vigil preceded these visits?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "26:219/q08/p1", "position": "The Prophet and companions had been obliged to keep night vigil before the duty was lifted.", "reasons": "Bursevī calls this the sounder view and relates the lifting to the five prayers on the Night Journey; he also reports Ibn ʿAbbās saying earlier prophets had the same obligation."}]}
{"id": "26:219/q09", "question": "Does this verse attest congregational prayer in the Qur'an?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "26:219/q09/p1", "position": "Yes; the Prophet's turning among prostrators was cited as its Qur'anic mention.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī and al-Nasafī report Muqātil reciting this verse when Abū Ḥanīfa could not recall a proof; Abū Ḥayyān instead reports Abū Ḥanīfa citing the verse after Muqātil's question."}]}
{"id": "26:219/q10", "question": "What does the lineage interpretation imply about the faith of the Prophet's forebears?", "turns_on": "Whether 'prostrators' proves every ancestor's belief, whether 'father' Āzar can mean another relative, and the force of the pure-lineage report.", "positions": [{"id": "26:219/q10/p1", "position": "It supports the belief that his ancestors were monotheists or believers, his lineage passing through pure, lawful unions.", "reasons": "The Rāfiḍa infer believing ancestors from descent among prostrators, cite the report of pure loins and wombs and 9:28 on unbelievers' impurity, and explain Āzar in 6:74 as Abraham's uncle or maternal forefather: Ishmael is called Jacob's sons' father in 2:133, the Prophet called al-ʿAbbās father, and Jesus belongs to Abraham's descendants in 6:84–85. Al-Ṭabrisī and al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī report lawful marriage and no fornication."}, {"id": "26:219/q10/p2", "position": "The verse cannot establish universal ancestral belief against the apparent designation of Āzar as Abraham's father.", "reasons": "Rāzī rejects moving 'father' from its apparent meaning in 6:74, rejects assigning every sense to an ambiguous expression at once, and says a solitary pure-lineage report cannot outweigh the Qur'an. Ālūsī likewise withholds this verse as proof of the parents' faith, although he warns against confidently denying their belief; Bursevī notes that lineage through prophets allows nonprophetic ancestors."}]}
{"id": "26:219/q11", "question": "How does God's seeing here relate to what can exist or be known?", "turns_on": "Whether sight is distinct from knowledge and whether its object must exist externally.", "positions": [{"id": "26:219/q11/p1", "position": "Divine vision is an unveiling distinct from knowledge and can relate to things not yet externally existent.", "reasons": "Ālūsī reports the knowers' comparison with seeing the Resurrection in a dream, while saying the divine mode befits God's majesty. Al-Sulamī's al-Wāsiṭī reads pre-eternal vision of the cosmos, and al-Sulamī says the Prophet's lineage was seen in absence and existence."}, {"id": "26:219/q11/p2", "position": "Divine vision does not relate to nonexistent things.", "reasons": "Ālūsī attributes this to many theologians without settling it here."}, {"id": "26:219/q11/p3", "position": "Divine vision reduces to God's knowledge.", "reasons": "Ālūsī reports this view from some theologians and says the issue is discussed elsewhere."}]}
{"id": "26:219/q12", "question": "What reassurance follows from God seeing the Prophet here?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "26:219/q12/p1", "position": "God's awareness of his worship and state confirms support, sufficiency and protection, strengthening his reliance.", "reasons": "Al-Bayḍāwī connects it to power over enemies and help for allies; al-Biqāʿī says encompassing knowledge secures benefit and repels harm; Ālūsī says his state merits guardianship. Bursevī's inward source says awareness of the Beloved's sight makes worship's hardship light, even like carrying mountains."}]}
{"id": "26:219/q13", "question": "How does this phrase connect with its surrounding discourse?", "turns_on": "The scope of context considered: neighboring trust and care commands or the whole sūrah's closing discourse.", "positions": [{"id": "26:219/q13/p1", "position": "It follows divine mercy and the call to trust God by showing care for the Prophet and the believers.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī and al-Nasafī connect God's mercy and the Prophet's night worship; al-Biqāʿī ties the description to divine sufficiency after the trust command. Ibn ʿĀshūr says the compact pairing gives Muslims care alongside their Messenger. Iṣlāḥī links the Prophet's spiritual vigilance to the command of affection in 26:215 and compares Jesus urging disciples to stay awake in the Gospels."}, {"id": "26:219/q13/p2", "position": "It belongs to the sūrah's return to true Qur'anic warnings and the prophetic histories as signs for stubborn Quraysh.", "reasons": "Iṣlāḥī says the concluding discourse revisits the opening theme: punishment signs may come and earlier prophetic stories already furnish signs."}]}
{"id": "26:219/q14", "question": "How do the following divine names bear on God's seeing the Prophet?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "26:219/q14/p1", "position": "The All-Hearing covers what he says and the All-Knowing what he intends and does; hearing is a distinct attribute.", "reasons": "Rāzī argues that if hearing were merely knowledge of audible things, 'All-Knowing' would add nothing to 'All-Hearing.'"}]}
{"id": "27:8/q01", "question": "What does the pronoun in 'came to it' refer to?", "turns_on": "The nearest named antecedent is the fire; another reading supplies the tree of the scene.", "positions": [{"id": "27:8/q01/p1", "position": "The fire Moses had seen or thought he saw.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān and Ālūsī prefer the earlier explicit fire; Ibn ʿĀshūr says the feminine pronoun follows Moses' description of the appearance as fire."}, {"id": "27:8/q01/p2", "position": "The tree bearing the light.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān reports a green samur or ʿalayq tree which did not burn and seemed to recede; Ālūsī finds this antecedent implausible."}]}
{"id": "27:8/q02", "question": "What was the apparent fire Moses approached?", "turns_on": "Whether nār names Moses' initial impression, a physical veil, or spiritual light.", "positions": [{"id": "27:8/q02/p1", "position": "Divine light rather than ordinary fire.", "reasons": "Moses mistook light for fire, say Mawardī, the majority he reports, Ibn ʿAbbās and others, and many later sources. Qatāda calls it God's light; Muqātil the Lord's light. Ibn ʿĀshūr says only Moses saw this otherworldly light and his wife may have doubted him. The Study Quran notes Arabic nār can stand for nūr."}, {"id": "27:8/q02/p2", "position": "A real fire, or fire containing light.", "reasons": "Saʿīd ibn Jubayr lists God's veils of might, dominion, authority, fire, light, cloud and water, identifying this as the fire of the call. Baghawī and Biqāʿī connect it to the prophetic veil report; Mawardī records fire with light."}, {"id": "27:8/q02/p3", "position": "Prophetic spiritual illumination.", "reasons": "Asad reads it as the light God bestows on prophets and, alternatively, as God's own light at the core of illumination. The Turkish commentary reports his metaphorical reading."}]}

ree when Moses approached?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "27:8/q03/p1", "position": "A luminous fire or light appeared in a green tree without consuming it and drew Moses near.", "reasons": "Wahb describes a green ʿalayq branch whose flame grew as its greenery increased; Moses tried to take a branch, recoiled when the flame leaned toward him, then heard the call. Ibn Kathīr says its light reached heaven; Biqāʿī describes Moses following it into a ravine."}, {"id": "27:8/q03/p2", "position": "Moses' sheep repeatedly fled before he approached God's light.", "reasons": "Abū Ṣakhr gives the repeated flight of the sheep as the lead up to the encounter."}]}
{"id": "27:8/q04", "question": "Why does this account say jāʾahā rather than atāhā?", "turns_on": "Whether the verbs imply differing difficulty in the narrated settings.", "positions": [{"id": "27:8/q04/p1", "position": "Jāʾa fits the more arduous scene, whereas atā suggests easier arrival.", "reasons": "Al-Rāghib distinguishes easy atyan from broader majīʾ. Al-Sāmarrāʾī cites derivatives implying ease and 23:27, 50:19, 18:71, 18:74 for harder jāʾa. Naml's firmer promise, shihāb qabas, and mission to Pharaoh's dispersed people make its scene harder than Qaṣaṣ or Ṭā Hā; frequency of the verbs in the sūras also fits."}, {"id": "27:8/q04/p2", "position": "The parallel accounts use different verbs for Moses' arrival.", "reasons": "Al-Burhān contrasts Ṭā Hā's atāhā; al-Sāmarrāʾī contrasts Qaṣaṣ's atāhā and notes the broader comparison of parallel narratives."}]}
{"id": "27:8/q05", "question": "Who was called, and why is the caller left unnamed here?", "turns_on": "How the passive verb is supplied and whether its lack of an explicit caller serves suspense.", "positions": [{"id": "27:8/q05/p1", "position": "Moses was called by God; the passive first magnifies the call and creates suspense.", "reasons": "Biqāʿī says the unannounced caller creates suspense and the explanation signals the event's greatness; Iṣlāḥī says the passive magnifies the event. Abū Ḥayyān and Ālūsī prefer Moses as the passive subject. Ibn ʿAṭiyya says Moses sought directions; Qurṭubī compares the right side of the mountain in 19:52."}, {"id": "27:8/q05/p2", "position": "The passive subject is the phrase an būrika or an implicit 'calling'.", "reasons": "Zajjāj and Naḥḥās allow the whole phrase to be nominative passive subject; Samīn and Abū Ḥayyān also report an implied call explained by the following words. Al-Farrāʾ makes the case of an depend on whether Moses is supplied. Ibn ʿAṭiyya reports al-Zajjāj's nominative analysis, supplying an implicit nūdiya annahu."}]}
{"id": "27:8/q06", "question": "From where and in what manner did Moses hear the call?", "turns_on": "The reported source of the sound and the nature of divine speech.", "positions": [{"id": "27:8/q06/p1", "position": "God spoke and Moses heard speech from the direction of the tree, mountain, or fire.", "reasons": "Wahb says the call came from above; al-Suddī says God's speech came from heaven at the tree. Ibn ʿAṭiyya, Baghawī and Bursevī describe an audible call from the tree or mountain; Ibn ʿAbbās says it came from the light."}, {"id": "27:8/q06/p2", "position": "God created speech in the tree, and Moses heard it from there.", "reasons": "Al-Naqqāsh and al-Jubbāʾī give created speech in the tree as the explanation; al-Jubbāʾī places the tree in the fire and angels around it."}, {"id": "27:8/q06/p3", "position": "The call came from every direction and reached Moses through all his senses.", "reasons": "Biqāʿī reports this account without further proof."}, {"id": "27:8/q06/p4", "position": "Moses heard God's letters and sound directly behind the fire's veil.", "reasons": "Ālūsī says divine wisdom allowed disclosure in the desired fire form while divine might remains unlimited; he rejects the claim that al-Ashʿarī said Moses actually heard inner speech."}, {"id": "27:8/q06/p5", "position": "Divine speech may be heard without ordinary letters or sound, even though the ordinary voice is also a reported account.", "reasons": "Rāzī reports Sunni explanations: necessary knowledge on hearing an extraordinary attribute or a voice from the tree. Ālūsī cites the sacred hadith and 42:11 for extraordinary hearing; he says al-Māturīdī permits hearing nonsound exceptionally and Ibn al-Humām's impossibility concerns ordinary experience."}]}
{"id": "27:8/q07", "question": "How could Moses know the caller was God?", "turns_on": "Which sign can rule out a deceptive creature as caller.", "positions": [{"id": "27:8/q07/p1", "position": "A miraculous green tree burning without being consumed established the caller's identity.", "reasons": "Rāzī prefers this accompanying miracle. He rejects proofs from a human's inability to call from fire, since Satan could enter it, and from the voice's magnitude, since angelic or demonic capacities are unknown. The Transoxanian imams raise the epistemic question."}, {"id": "27:8/q07/p2", "position": "The extraordinary character of divine speech gave Moses necessary knowledge.", "reasons": "Rāzī reports this Sunni explanation: speech unlike letters or sounds is necessarily recognized as God's attribute."}, {"id": "27:8/q07/p3", "position": "No human can call from the fire or tree.", "reasons": "Rāzī reports and rejects this first Transoxanian proof because Satan could enter either and call."}, {"id": "27:8/q07/p4", "position": "The voice's magnitude proved its divine origin.", "reasons": "Rāzī rejects this second proof because the capacities of angels and devils are unknown."}]}
{"id": "27:8/q08", "question": "How is an in the call parsed?", "turns_on": "Whether the clause explains a speech act, nominalizes a call with omitted bi, or contracts emphatic anna; the last hinges on the separator rule for supplication.", "positions": [{"id": "27:8/q08/p1", "position": "It is explanatory: the call conveys speech, then its content follows.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī, Rāzī, Nasafī, grammarians, Ibn ʿĀshūr, and Ālūsī use the speech sense in nūdiya; Ālūsī prefers it. Al-Raḍī says this is necessary if būrika is a prayer, but Ālūsī rejects the claimed consensus. Biqāʿī says it directs the listener to the clarification."}, {"id": "27:8/q08/p2", "position": "It is a verbal noun particle, with an omitted preposition after nūdiya.", "reasons": "Zajjāj and Naḥḥās describe the resulting accusative construction; al-Farrāʾ relates case to whether Moses is implicit. Abū Ḥayyān, Samīn, Bursevī and Ālūsī give the omitted preposition analysis. Al-Kashf objects that an optative verbal noun would not announce good news, an objection Ālūsī questions."}, {"id": "27:8/q08/p3", "position": "It is lightened from anna, with an implied pronoun of the affair.", "reasons": "Bayḍāwī and Nasafī say prayer permits the absent separator; Abū Ḥayyān replies to Zamakhsharī that qad is not used with a supplication. Samīn notes the difficulty of a prayer as its predicate. Ālūsī reports rule exceptions and disputes al-Raḍī's consensus. Ibn ʿAṭiyya reports al-Zajjāj's nominative parse with an implicit nūdiya annahu."}]}
{"id": "27:8/q09", "question": "How is the nūn in an būrika pronounced?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "27:8/q09/p1", "position": "Before bāʾ the silent nūn becomes a concealed mīm with nasalization, without assimilation.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jazarī says there is no disagreement here; al-Dānī's reported dispute concerns original silent mīm before bāʾ. {"id": "27:8/q13", "question": "Who or what is blessed as 'the one in the fire'?", "turns_on": "Whether man is personal or nonpersonal; whether 'in' is literal location, nearness, ellipsis for place or divine power, or a spiritual reading.", "positions": [{"id": "27:8/q13/p1", "position": "God, disclosed by His light and speech, without spatial enclosure.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn Jubayr, al-Ḥasan and others are reported to identify God; reports say His light was in the tree or that He called from light. Baghawī cites a Torah description of God's coming from Sinai, Seir and Paran, associating them with Moses, Jesus and Muhammad and Paran with Mecca. Thaʿlabī and Rāzī likewise read the phrase as God's greeting to Moses, with angels around him. Qurṭubī reports an omitted fī or nearby location. Ṭabāṭabāʾī finds Moses among those around the fire in the Ṭā Hā parallel, but reports his placement inside as another view."}, {"id": "27:8/q13/p3", "position": "Angels stationed in the fire or light.", "reasons": "Al-Suddī says angels were inside; Naḥḥās reports Qatāda naming both inner and outer groups angels. Ibn ʿAṭiyya also reports Ibn ʿAbbās identifying man as the light."}, {"id": "27:8/q13/p5", "position": "The fire itself.", "reasons": "Mujāhid and Ibn ʿAbbās report this repeatedly. Ibn ʿAṭiyya transmits Ibn Jinnī's reading tabārakat al-nār wa-man ḥawlahā, which directly names the fire as blessed."}, {"id": "27:8/q13/p6", "position": "The location of the fire, the blessed plot or valley; in its widest sense the Syrian region.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī, Bayḍāwī and Ālūsī take an implied place and sometimes all its inhabitants. Bursawī adds the fertility poem."}, {"id": "27:8/q13/p7", "position": "God's power, authority, dominion, or proof manifested there.", "reasons": "Thaʿlabī, Wāḥidī, Ṭabrisī and others supply an omitted noun; Abū Ḥayyān says sound God-referent reports must be read this way. {"id": "27:8/q15", "question": "Why is blessing announced at the start of the call?", "turns_on": "Whether blessing functions as a greeting, announces a sanctified event and place, or carries optative force.", "positions": [{"id": "27:8/q15/p1", "position": "It honors and greets Moses and the angels, reassuring him before his commission.", "reasons": "Thaʿlabī, Wāḥidī, Baghawī, Ṭabrisī, Ibn al-Jawzī and Qurṭubī compare the greeting of Abraham's household in 11:73. {"id": "27:8/q17", "question": "What does the glorification assert or do?", "turns_on": "Whether the primary force is divine transcendence, wonder at the event, or inward purification.", "positions": [{"id": "27:8/q17/p1", "position": "It declares God free of defect, evil, created likeness, embodiment and spatial limits.", "reasons": "Zajjāj and language scholars define subḥān as exalting God above evil; Wāḥidī, Baghawī and Abū ʿUbayd say imperfection. Bayḍāwī, Abū Ḥayyān, Bursevī, Ālūsī, Ṭabāṭabāʾī and Iṣlāḥī use it to block a localizing or humanizing inference from the fire and speech. Ibn ʿAṭiyya says this declaration rules out likeness or modality in the divine call on either account of its speaker."}, {"id": "27:8/q17/p2", "position": "It expresses wonder and announces that the Lord of all worlds wills this momentous event.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī, Rāzī, Bayḍāwī, Bursevī, Ālūsī and Elmalılı connect the phrase with the encounter's greatness; Biqāʿī says lordship reflects God's complete essence and acts, including His care for Moses as child and adult. Iṣlāḥī urges trust in the universal Lord's providence."}, {"id": "27:8/q17/p3", "position": "Inwardly, it transcends the essence by shedding psychic traits and bodily veils.", "reasons": "Qāshānī's inward reading includes relinquishing defects and faults."}]}
{"id": "27:8/q18", "question": "What does calling God 'Lord of the worlds' contribute?", "turns_on": "Whether the title explains this call's universal authority or the different emphases of parallel scenes.", "positions": [{"id": "27:8/q18/p1", "position": "It shows universal lordship, power, providence and fitness for glorification.", "reasons": "Biqāʿī connects the perfect Lord's acts with raising Moses. {"id": "27:8/q21", "question": "How does this call compare with the parallel Moses narratives?", "turns_on": "Which detail in the parallel telling carries each account's rhetorical emphasis.", "positions": [{"id": "27:8/q21/p1", "position": "Naml gives the blessing and glorification, while Qaṣaṣ specifies where the call came from.", "reasons": "Al-Sāmarrāʾī says Naml's added formula suits its exalted setting; Qaṣaṣ supplies geographical detail for its fuller mode.
